source: We subsequently showed that TSR2 silencing incurs the same effect on RAN translation efficiency as the direct depletion of RPS26 and the observed regulation does not stem from global translation inhibition (Figure 5A&C).
evidence: This is a finding from the TSR2 knockdown experiments, supported by Figure 5A and 5C.

claim: It remains unclear whether the effect of TSR2 silencing on RAN translation is due to hampering RPS26 loading to the 40 S subunit or a consequence of decrease of RPS26 level.
source: However, it remains unclear whether this is an effect of hampering RPS26 loading to the 40 S subunit by TSR2 depletion, or a consequence of decrease of RPS26 level.
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertainty regarding the mechanism of TSR2's effect on RAN translation.

claim: The silencing of TSR2 exhibited selectivity towards FMRpolyG over the FMRP reading frame without affecting the other 40 S ribosomal proteins.
source: The silencing of this chaperone also exhibited selectivity towards FMRpolyG over the FMRP reading frame without affecting the other 40 S ribosomal proteins, such as RACK1, RPS6, and RPS15 (Figure 5A&B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TSR2 knockdown experiments, supported by Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Tsr2 is responsible for replacing damaged Rps26, which undergoes oxidation on mature 80 S ribosomes under stress conditions.
source: Previously, it was shown that Tsr2 is responsible for replacing damaged Rps26, which undergoes oxidation on mature 80 S ribosomes under stress conditions (Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Tsr2 function in replacing oxidized Rps26.

claim: The activity of TSR2 chaperone may play an important role in modulating RAN translation via Rps26 assembly or disassembly from ribosomal subunits, also during different stresses.
source: Therefore, the activity of this chaperone may play an important role in modulating RAN translation via Rps26 assembly or disassembly from ribosomal subunits, also during different stresses (Yang and Karbstein, 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and cited knowledge about TSR2 function.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding RPS26 and TSR2 were associated with hematopoiesis impairment that underlies the genetic blood disorder Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA).
source: Importantly, we provided additional evidence that RPS26 specifically affects CGGexp-related RAN translation, as the depletion of another 40 S ribosomal protein, RPS6, did not affect the FMRpolyG biosynthesis (Figure 5C). Moreover, mutations in genes encoding RPS26 and TSR2 were associated with hematopoiesis impairment that underlies the genetic blood disorder Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) (Piantanida et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023; Doherty et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the association of RPS26 and TSR2 mutations with Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

claim: Analyses of DBA patient cells and RPS26-depleted HeLa cells found alterations in ribosome biogenesis and pre-rRNA processing.
source: Previously, analyses of DBA patient cells and RPS26-depleted HeLa cells found alterations in ribosome biogenesis and pre-rRNA processing (Doherty et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the effects of RPS26 depletion on ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Proteins implicated in the eukaryotic PIC and components of large ribosomal subunits were altered upon RPS26 silencing in HEK293T cells.
source: Similarly, we found that proteins implicated in the eukaryotic PIC and components of large ribosomal subunits were altered upon RPS26 silencing in HEK293T cells (Figure 4B), suggesting rearrangements in ribosomal composition.
evidence: This is a finding from the SILAC-MS proteomic analysis, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: RPS25 knockdown resulted in changes in abundance of ribosomal components.
source: Similar observation was noted in case of RPS25 knockdown which resulted in changes in abundance of ribosomal components (Luan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the effects of RPS25 knockdown on ribosomal components.

claim: Mutants of 40 S components accumulate more 60 S subunits.
source: Hence, our data is consistent with the fact that mutants of 40 S components accumulates more 60 S subunits (Cheng et al., 2019) and the knockdown of 40 S ribosomal proteins elicits the enhanced translation of 60 S ribosomal proteins (Luan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the relationship between 40 S and 60 S subunit levels.

claim: The knockdown of 40 S ribosomal proteins elicits the enhanced translation of 60 S ribosomal proteins.
source: Hence, our data is consistent with the fact that mutants of 40 S components accumulates more 60 S subunits (Cheng et al., 2019) and the knockdown of 40 S ribosomal proteins elicits the enhanced translation of 60 S ribosomal proteins (Luan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the compensatory response to 40 S ribosomal protein depletion.

claim: The data supports the evidence regarding co-dependent regulation of stability and accumulation of 40 S and 60 S ribosomal proteins.
source: Altogether, our data supports the evidence regarding co-dependent regulation of stability and accumulation of 40 S and 60 S ribosomal proteins (Gregory et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and cited knowledge about ribosomal protein regulation.

claim: RPS26 is highly expressed in ovarian cells and was shown to be important for female fertility.
source: Moreover, RPS26 is highly expressed in ovarian cells and was shown to be important for female fertility (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about RPS26 expression and function in ovarian cells.

claim: RPS26 is necessary for oocyte growth and follicle development, and its depletion causes changes in transcription and chromatin configuration, leading to premature ovarian failure.
source: It is necessary for oocyte growth and follicle development, and its depletion causes changes in transcription and chromatin configuration, leading to premature ovarian failure (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the role of RPS26 in ovarian function.

claim: The discovery that RPS26 regulates the level of FMRpolyG in cellular models sheds new light on the potential role of RPS26-related RAN translation in FXPOI.
source: Our discovery that RPS26 regulates the level of FMRpolyG in cellular models sheds new light on the potential role of RPS26-related RAN translation in FXPOI, where FMRpolyG aggregates are detected in ovarian cells and contribute to the development and progression of fertility issues (Buijsen et al., 2016; Shelly et al., 2021; Rosario et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and cited knowledge about FMRpolyG in FXPOI.

claim: FMRpolyG aggregates are detected in ovarian cells and contribute to the development and progression of fertility issues in FXPOI.
source: Our discovery that RPS26 regulates the level of FMRpolyG in cellular models sheds new light on the potential role of RPS26-related RAN translation in FXPOI, where FMRpolyG aggregates are detected in ovarian cells and contribute to the development and progression of fertility issues (Buijsen et al., 2016; Shelly et al., 2021; Rosario et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about FMRpolyG in FXPOI.

claim: The depletion of RPS26 from 40 S subunits contributes to its specialization and modulates the translation of specific mRNAs.
source: Given these findings, it is likely that the depletion of RPS26 from 40 S subunits contributes to its specialization and modulates the translation of specific mRNAs (Yang and Karbstein, 2022; Ferretti et al., 2017; Li et al., 2022; Gaikwad et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and cited knowledge about ribosome specialization.

claim: Nearly 400 proteins responding to RPS26 depletion were identified, which is similar to ca. 500 mRNAs for which translation rate was altered upon Rps26 insufficiency in yeast.
source: Remarkably, our experiments identified nearly 400 proteins responding to RPS26 depletion, which is similar to ca. 500 mRNAs, for which translation rate was altered upon Rps26 insufficiency in yeast (Gaikwad et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison of the experimental findings with cited knowledge about Rps26 effects in yeast.

claim: Depletion or mutations in RPS26 resulted in the reduction of 40 S subunits level.
source: In fact, depletion or mutations in RPS26 resulted in the reduction of 40 S subunits level (Gaikwad et al., 2021; Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023); however, overall translation rate was not impacted by RPS26 impairment (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the effects of RPS26 depletion on 40 S subunit levels.

claim: Overall translation rate was not impacted by RPS26 impairment.
source: In fact, depletion or mutations in RPS26 resulted in the reduction of 40 S subunits level (Gaikwad et al., 2021; Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023); however, overall translation rate was not impacted by RPS26 impairment (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the lack of global translation inhibition upon RPS26 depletion.

claim: RPS26 depletion did not elicit global translation inhibition, which strengthens the conclusion that decrease of polyglycine production is not a byproduct of global translation shut down but rather the specific response to RPS26 deficiency.
source: We also observed that RPS26 depletion did not elicit global translation inhibition (Figure 2B), which additionally strengthens our conclusion that decrease of polyglycine production is not a byproduct of global translation shut down but rather the specific response to RPS26 deficiency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SUnSET assay results, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The observed effect of RPS26 depletion may be explained by the decrease of translationally active ribosomes, which impacts the translation rate of selected mRNAs, including upstream ORF of FMR1.
source: Alternatively, the observed effect may be explained by the decrease of translationally active ribosomes, which in return, impacts the translation rate of selected mRNAs, including upstream ORF of FMR1.
evidence: This is an alternative explanation for the observed effects of RPS26 depletion.

claim: RPS26 insufficiency resulted in the decrease of mammalian cells viability.
source: In fact, it was shown that RPS26 insufficiency resulted in the decrease of mammalian cells viability (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023), which is in line with our analysis regarding cells proliferation upon RPS26 silencing (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is cited knowledge that is consistent with the experimental findings, supported by Figure 2A.

claim: RPS6 and RPS25 depletion negatively impacted cells proliferation.
source: Moreover, RPS6 and RPS25 depletion also negatively impacted cells proliferation (Figures 5D and 6B), which is consistent with previously described data linking the ribosomal proteins deficiencies (both from 40 S and 60 S subunits) with a cellular growth rate inhibition (Cheng et al., 2019; Luan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from the cell proliferation assays, supported by Figures 5D and 6B, and consistent with cited knowledge.

claim: Ribosomal proteins deficiencies (both from 40 S and 60 S subunits) are linked with cellular growth rate inhibition.
source: Moreover, RPS6 and RPS25 depletion also negatively impacted cells proliferation (Figures 5D and 6B), which is consistent with previously described data linking the ribosomal proteins deficiencies (both from 40 S and 60 S subunits) with a cellular growth rate inhibition (Cheng et al., 2019; Luan et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the effects of ribosomal protein deficiencies on cell growth.

claim: The C-terminal domain of RPS26 is essential for mRNA interaction.
source: It has been shown that the C-terminal domain of RPS26 is essential for mRNA interaction (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023), although whether RPS26 recognizes specific sequential or structural motifs within the mRNA remains unclear.
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the structural requirements for RPS26-mRNA interaction.

claim: Whether RPS26 recognizes specific sequential or structural motifs within the mRNA remains unclear.
source: It has been shown that the C-terminal domain of RPS26 is essential for mRNA interaction (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023), although whether RPS26 recognizes specific sequential or structural motifs within the mRNA remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge regarding RPS26-mRNA recognition.

claim: Data derived from yeast models suggest that nucleotides in positions −1 to −10 upstream of the AUG codon, especially Kozak sequence elements, play an important role in Rps26 interactions and translation efficiency.
source: Data derived from yeast models suggest that nucleotides in positions −1 to −10 upstream of the AUG codon, especially Kozak sequence elements, play an important role in Rps26 interactions and translation efficiency (Ferretti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about Rps26-mRNA interactions in yeast.

claim: According to the established ribosome-mRNA structure, RPS26 contacts with mRNA upstream to AUG codon and the C-terminus reaches into mRNA exit channel.
source: According to the established ribosome-mRNA structure, RPS26 contacts with mRNA upstream to AUG codon and the C-terminus reaches into mRNA exit channel (Anger et al., 2013; Hussain et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about the structural positioning of RPS26 on the ribosome.

claim: Recent findings indicate that in eukaryotic cells, positions −11 to −16 upstream of the start codon might be more significant for RNA recognition, stabilizing PIC, and translation initiation.
source: Recent findings indicate that in eukaryotic cells, positions −11 to −16 upstream of the start codon might be more significant for RNA recognition, stabilizing PIC, and translation initiation (Havkin-Solomon et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about RPS26-mRNA interactions in eukaryotic cells.

claim: Bioinformatic analysis of proteins sensitive to RPS26 depletion revealed that their transcripts were GC-rich (especially in the 5'UTR region) and enriched with k-mers mainly consisting of Gs and Cs.
source: Our bioinformatic analysis of proteins sensitive to RPS26 depletion revealed that their transcripts were GC-rich (especially in the 5'UTR region) and enriched with k-mers mainly consisting of Gs and Cs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); however, we did not identify the importance of any specific sequence positions from AUG codon.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioinformatic analysis, supported by Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The bioinformatic analysis did not identify the importance of any specific sequence positions from AUG codon.
source: Our bioinformatic analysis of proteins sensitive to RPS26 depletion revealed that their transcripts were GC-rich (especially in the 5'UTR region) and enriched with k-mers mainly consisting of Gs and Cs (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1); however, we did not identify the importance of any specific sequence positions from AUG codon.
evidence: This is a finding from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The fact that FMR1 5'UTR is a GC-rich sequence (~90%) suggests that RPS26 level-sensitive translation is selective for transcripts rich with GC nucleotides.
source: These data and the fact that FMR1 5'UTR is a GC-rich sequence (~90%) suggest that RPS26 level-sensitive translation is selective for transcripts rich with GC nucleotides.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bioinformatic analysis and the characteristics of FMR1 5'UTR.

claim: RPS25 depletion in the Drosophila C9orf72 model and in induced motor neurons derived from C9-ALS/FTD patients alleviated toxicity caused by RAN translation.
source: The depletion of RPS25 in the Drosophila C9orf72 model, and in induced motor neurons derived from C9-ALS/FTD patients, alleviated toxicity caused by RAN translation (Yamada et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about RPS25 as a RAN translation modifier in C9-ALS/FTD models.

claim: In FXTAS Drosophila model, RPS25 knockdown led to enhancement of CGG repeats-related toxicity.
source: On the contrary, in FXTAS Drosophila model, RPS25 knockdown led to enhancement of CGG repeats-related toxicity; however, underlying mechanism was not determined (Linsalata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about RPS25 effects in FXTAS Drosophila model.

claim: The downregulation of RPS26 and RPS25 affects FMRpolyG biosynthesis.
source: Altogether, we have identified two ribosomal proteins, RPS26 and RPS25 as modifiers of CGGexp-related RAN translation of mutant FMR1 mRNA, which imply that the downregulation of these two 40 S ribosomal proteins affects FMRpolyG biosynthesis.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: RPS26 depletion alleviated toxicity caused by FMRpolyG but did not affect FMRP.
source: Importantly, we demonstrated that RPS26 depletion alleviated toxicity caused by FMRpolyG but did not affect FMRP, the main product of the FMR1 gene.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings showing selective effects of RPS26 depletion.

claim: Sequence/structure elements within FMR1 mRNA, which make this transcript sensitive to the level of studied ribosomal proteins, may be potential therapeutic targets.
source: This suggests that sequence/structure elements within FMR1 mRNA, which make this transcript sensitive to the level of studied ribosomal proteins, may be potential therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings about the therapeutic potential of targeting RPS26-sensitive elements.
